bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body: Geopolitical supply chain disruptions (Middle East/Iran) keeping PP prices elevated (new normal USD 1,200-1,350/ton); Customer inventory correction delaying volume uptake; Labor availability/skilling for stitching operations (key bottleneck); Europe dependency (56% exports) though diversified within region.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Disciplined, pragmatic, and strategically patient; emphasizing 'quality of business' over pure volume; confident in pass-through mechanisms and long-term customer stickiness; cautious on short-term order book but bullish on medium-term consumption trends.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body: Margin driver is 'stitching minutes' not just tonnage (labor efficiency is the real constraint); DFIA reversal was a regulatory artifact, not operational failure; Non-woven uses imported fiber (no captive yarn), creating a different supply chain dynamic than FIBC; Japan strategy is about long-term diversification and first-mover branding, not immediate margin accretion.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- States a disciplined, capability-aligned diversification and capital-allocation philosophy — investing only where it extends existing capabilities.
- Prioritises brownfield, fast-payback investments while maintaining balance-sheet strength and credit discipline.
- Inorganic capital deployed selectively into Europe — a UK acquisition and an Italian JV — to gain closer customer engagement, better pricing control and faster product development.
- A 2:1 bonus issue was made in 2016 (the only shareholder-return action mentioned in the deck).
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Vertically integrated manufacturing from polymer processing, flat tape, fabric production, MFY yarns and UV masterbatch through to conversion into FIBCs and small bags, which the company says enhances cost management, operational agility and consistent quality
- Over 50 years in industrial bulk packaging and 30+ years of export experience; first company in North India to produce HDPE woven sacks in the early 1970s and among the first Indian exporters of PP woven sacks to Europe in the late 1980s
- Export-driven model with presence in more than 40 countries; exports contribute approximately 75% of manufacturing revenue, and the share of USA in FIBC exports dropped only marginally despite US tariffs, offset by deeper EU penetration
- Low customer concentration — no single customer contributes over 5% of revenue
- Approximately 80% repeat business and more than 2,500 customised packaging configurations under a B2B distributor-led model
- Certification depth (BRCGS A+, HACCP, SEDEX, Kosher, Halal) plus a dedicated cleanroom for food-grade FIBC, enabling access to regulated, premium and value-added segments
- Proprietary in-house ERP system enabling real-time monitoring, traceability and process-driven decision-making across manufacturing and supply chain
- Renewable energy base — rooftop solar plus long-term power purchase agreements, with solar sources now accounting for more than 55% of total electricity consumption (MD&A); the company was the first in Uttar Pradesh to install rooftop solar in early 2014
- Sustainability positioning: zero liquid discharge, rainwater harvesting, EPR compliance and all product lines designed to be 100% recyclable
- Third-generation promoter leadership with continuity in the Agarwal family (Manoj Agarwal as Chairman cum Managing Director)
- Credit ratings of Crisil BBB+ stable for long-term facilities and Crisil A2 for short-term facilities, described by the Chairman as an upgrade reflecting a strong financial risk profile
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Raw material price volatility (polypropylene-based inputs) — MD&A lists "Volatile raw material prices" as an industry restraint, and the Board's Risk Management section states the Company "continues to manage operational risks such as fluctuations in foreign exchange rates and raw material prices, which are monitored and addressed on an ongoing basis". As a converter of PP into FIBCs, fabrics and yarn, resin cost swings hit the spread directly.
- Foreign exchange rate fluctuation — Explicitly named by the Board as an ongoing operational risk, and structurally amplified by the export-led model — the Company reports an "established international presence across 40+ countries, with exports contributing 75%". Realisations and margins are therefore currency-translated rather than domestic-rupee.
- Export and geographic concentration in USA / Canada / EU — Exports are the dominant revenue channel, and the addressed market is itself concentrated: global FIBC trade in 2025 is estimated at over US$ 1.75 billion, "65% of which is accounted for by imports within the USA, Canada & the EU countries". Demand or policy shocks in a small set of destination markets transmit straight to the order book.
- Tariff regimes, trade-policy shifts and geopolitical disruption — MD&A notes "evolving tariff structures and geopolitical developments may continue to influence sourcing strategies across international markets", alongside Russia-Ukraine and West Asia conflicts driving "supply chain disruptions, elevated energy prices, increased shipping costs and uncertainty in global trade". China's declining FIBC export share is itself attributed to tariff-related developments — the same lever can move against India.
- Competition from emerging low-cost FIBC supply bases — The Company records "shifting sourcing patterns, with countries such as Vietnam and Bangladesh increasing their market presence, particularly in North America". India currently supplies nearly 78.2% of US FIBC imports, 50.0% of Canada and 66.4% of the EU — a high share that new origins can erode.
- Tightening environmental regulation of plastics — MD&A lists "Stringent environmental regulations on plastic markets" as a restraint and notes governments "progressively reinforcing policy frameworks" that are "influencing material choices, reshaping production processes, industry dynamics and long-term investment decisions". India has introduced stricter plastic-waste rules; the Company states its "export production remains outside the ambit of these regulatory contitions [sic]", so the exposure sits mainly on domestic volumes.
- Product concentration in FIBC / industrial bulk packaging and business cyclicality — FIBC alone is 53.29% of the revenue mix (43.33% of volume mix), with fabric a further 24.27% — the portfolio is single-family. Management's own rationale for the B2C/value-added pivot is that it "will help diversify revenue streams, reduce business cyclicality, strengthen resilience", implicitly acknowledging cyclicality in the existing base. Customer concentration is the offsetting positive: "No single customer contributes over 5% of revenue".
- Execution risk on the diversification build-out (non-woven greenfield + Taslan yarn JV) — The Company is "establishing a dedicated greenfield manufacturing facility to manufacture non-woven fabrics, using needle-punching technology" and entered a JV for premium PP Taslan yarn at 1,000 MT/year capacity, with "technology ownership post-transfer". These are named as "key growth drivers for the Company in the years ahead" — both are new segments outside the five-decade core, so ramp, technology transfer and market-entry execution carry the growth narrative.

business.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers

business.body:
- Presents itself as a cost-effective, custom-engineered industrial packaging company with a core focus on FIBCs (jumbo bags) and technical textiles, built on 50+ years of operations and 30+ years of export experience.
- Export-led model with ~70% of manufacturing revenue from international markets across 40+ countries, Europe being the largest market and 80-85% of business coming as repeat orders from long-standing customers.
- Frames FIBC as 'FIBC economics, not commodity packaging' — pricing is driven by specifications, compliance and customisation rather than volumes, with increasing focus on value-added applications.
- Diversified end-market exposure spanning food industry (44%), industrial packaging (23%), construction (12%), agriculture (8%), automotive (7%) and mining/minerals including chemicals (6%) of revenue.
- Carries a CRISIL A2 short-term / BBB+ long-term credit rating and states full compliance with global regulatory standards (BRCGS A+, UN-certified and food/pharma-grade options).

- [Market entry] Entered Japan as a market in 2024 and started manufacturing high-tenacity PP multifilament yarn the same year.
- [Leadership] Describes a generational transition, with a new generation now leading a 50-year-old business around innovation, sustainability and growth.
- [Export mix] Continent-wise exports concentrated in Europe (59.4%), followed by South America (19.4%) and North America (16.1%), with Asia, Australia and Africa marginal.
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: Established in 1971, Kanpur Plastipack Limited (KPL) is a vertically integrated manufacturer, exporter and packaging-solutions provider whose chain runs from polymer processing and flat tape through fabric, multifilament yarn and UV masterbatch into finished Flexible Intermediate Bulk Containers (FIBCs) and small bags. It sells through a B2B distributor-led model offering more than 2,500 customised packaging configurations to customers in chemicals, food, agriculture, pharmaceuticals, construction and mining across Europe, the Americas, Asia-Pacific, Africa and Australia, and also operates Dealer Operated Polymer Warehouses (DOPW) for Indian Oil Corporation Limited at Kanpur and Bareilly. During FY 2025-26 the loss-making CPP division was disposed of in Q1, a 76.19% stake in UK FIBC distributor Valex Ventures Limited was acquired, and a 50:50 joint venture, Essekan Private Limited, was incorporated with Essegomma S.p.A. of Italy for premium PP Taslan yarn; other subsidiaries are Bright Choice Ventures Private Limited and Kanplas Earning Solutions Private Limited (both wholly owned).
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **Industrial bulk packaging (FIBC):** Flexible Intermediate Bulk Containers (FIBCs), also known as Jumbo bags, Food-grade FIBCs produced in a dedicated cleanroom facility, Small bags / PP woven sacks
- **Fabrics and yarn:** PP woven fabrics, GEO fabric, Liners and tape, PP Multi-filament Yarn (MFY)
- **Additives:** UV Masterbatches
- **Other custom products:** Filler cords, Liners, Specialised textile products for small-scale, custom and tender-based production
- **Technical textiles (under development):** Non-woven fabrics using needle-punching technology (greenfield project), Premium PP Taslan yarn via the ESSEKAN 50:50 JV with Essegomma S.p.A.
- **Polymer distribution:** Dealer Operated Polymer Warehouse (DOPW) of Indian Oil Corporation Limited

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Strengthen and scale the core FIBC segment, which the Company calls the foundation of its business, through the capacity expansion undertaken during the year at Unit III, Gajner Road (construction of a building plus installation of plant & machinery), with the stated objective of increasing exposure to FIBCs because they carry higher margins and value addition.
- Raise the share of food-grade, premium and customized FIBCs in the portfolio to cater to evolving customer and industry dynamics, improving product mix rather than chasing topline alone (management frames FY26 as focused on 'better product mix, stronger customer relationships, and sustainable realizations').
- Diversify from a primarily FIBC-focused company into a diversified technical textiles enterprise by setting up a greenfield non-woven manufacturing facility using needle-punch technology, targeting automotive interiors, geo-textiles, agriculture, artificial leather, exhibition carpets/carpets and shoe insoles; the existing building from the erstwhile CPP division is to be reused for this project, and capacity is to be scaled in a phased manner based on market demand.
- Expand into premium polypropylene (PP) yarns and technical textile solutions through ESSEKAN Private Limited, a 50:50 joint venture in India with M/s Essegomma S.p.A., Italy — the Company's first ever JV — combining global technological expertise and brand strength with KPL's existing Multi Filament Yarn manufacturing base and market presence, to sell speciality PP Taslan yarn into domestic and export markets and to diversify into outdoor and lifestyle textiles, furniture, upholstery and other high-performance end uses beyond traditional industrial applications.
- Use the premium PP yarn and technical textiles expansion as a foray into high-growth adjacent B2C-linked segments described as less cyclical, more specification-driven and offering better margin visibility; the Essegomma JV is framed as entry into the luxury retail-consumer segment of modern India.
- Build direct European market presence through the completed acquisition of a 76% holding in M/s Valex Ventures Limited, United Kingdom, from Chairman & Managing Director Mr. Manoj Agarwal, enabling closer customer engagement, improved market access and enhanced capability to serve regulated customers, and expected over the medium to long term to strengthen export positioning and support growth in UK markets.
- Add capacity in the weaving section and the Multi Filament Yarn (MFY) division to cater to future requirements of those segments, and create/upgrade additional infrastructure facilities to improve operational efficiencies and production facilities.
- Pursue phased expansion into non-woven and specialty textiles aligned with existing capabilities, supported by prudent capital allocation through brownfield investments, faster-payback projects and continued balance-sheet discipline.
- Run a scalable lean model in which growth is shaped by operating leverage, higher throughput and skilled workforce deployment rather than capital-intensive expansion, with close monitoring of cash flows, working capital efficiency and asset utilisation.
- Invest in people through focused skill development, training and capability-building while increasing automation across manufacturing processes to improve productivity, quality consistency, operational efficiency and scalability.
- Strengthen operational readiness via increased focus on safety, process standardization, automation and warehouse expansion, aimed at optimising operating costs (Opex) and improving On Time In Full (OTIF) delivery performance; traceability systems are used to reinforce quality assurance and customer confidence particularly in regulated and export-oriented markets, complemented by continued investment in digital tools and lean processes.
- Sustain the export-driven model — exports are approximately 75% of manufacturing revenues across a presence in more than 40 geographies — with deeper customer engagement and improved market access, and a B2B distributor-led model offering more than 2,500 customized packaging configurations.
- Maintain vertically integrated manufacturing spanning polymer processing, flat tape, fabric production, MFY yarns and UV masterbatch culminating in conversion to FIBCs and small bags, to enhance cost management, operational agility and consistent quality; FIBC-led growth is pursued by increasingly converting fabric output into finished FIBC products with improved margins.
- Embed sustainability-led efficiency in the growth roadmap through renewable energy adoption, efficient resource utilisation and cost optimisation, alongside zero liquid discharge, rainwater harvesting, recyclable product design and plastic waste recycling across facilities.
- Consolidate and build on the recovery in the Dealer Operated Polymer Warehouse (DOPW) activity of Indian Oil Corporation Limited by further consolidating market position and enhancing service delivery in the coming periods, following the new DOP warehouse opened at Bareily in the previous year.
- Complete the strategic exit from the CPP Division — disposed in Q1 as a decision to shut down the loss-making unit — allowing focus on improving operations and seeking alternate markets.
- Committed to zero liquid discharge, rainwater harvesting, and EPR compliance (stated under "Sustainable Operations"; no target date disclosed in the routed text)
- All product lines are designed to be 100% recyclable (standing product-design commitment; no target date disclosed in the routed text)
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: KPL's expansion in FY 2025-26 runs along three tracks: brownfield FIBC capacity, a greenfield technical-textiles diversification, and inorganic/JV additions. During the year the Company undertook a capacity expansion at Unit III, Gajner Road, comprising construction of a building along with installation of plant & machinery; management states the FIBC expansion at Unit 3 "will add up to 1,200 MT by the end of current year and up to 6,000 MT per annum over the period of five years", with the MD&A adding that the expansion "is progressing as planned" and is intended to lift value addition, capacity utilisation and the share of food-grade, premium and customized FIBCs. Alongside, the Company proposes to add capacity in its weaving section and in the Multi Filament Yarn (MFY) division to serve future requirements of those segments, and says additional infrastructure facilities have been created and upgraded to improve operational efficiencies and production facilities, together with warehouse expansion and increased automation across manufacturing processes. The second track is diversification into technical textiles: the Company has undertaken to establish a greenfield manufacturing facility for "Non-Woven Fabrics" based on needle-punching technology, targeted at automotive interiors, agriculture, geo-textiles, artificial leather, shoe insoles, exhibition carpets and carpets. The existing building available from the erstwhile CPP division is to be re-used for this project; plant and equipment was expected to start arriving from June 2026 onwards with commercial production to start by September 2026 (the Chairman/MD message places commercial production as targeted to commence from FY 2026-27, with capacity to be scaled in a phased manner based on market demand). The Directors' Report states that total expenditure on the non-woven project plus the capacity-expansion/infrastructure items "will amount to Rs 107 Cr and is expected to be completed by September, 2026", part-funded by a Rs 40 Cr term loan from Yes Bank. The third track is inorganic and collaborative: the Company completed the acquisition of a 76% holding in M/s Valex Ventures Limited, United Kingdom from its Chairman & Managing Director, giving direct presence in the European/UK market, and entered its first-ever joint venture with M/s Essegomma S.p.A., Italy for high-performance polypropylene yarns and technical textile solutions through ESSEKAN Private Limited, a 50:50 India JV, where machines have been erected, trials conducted and "Sales shall begin this fiscal"; the corporate-overview page for the premium PP Taslan yarn line states 1,000 MT/year capacity. In the trading business, an additional Dealer Operated Polymer Warehouse (DOPW) of IOCL at Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh began operation, and both DOPWs (Kanpur and Bareilly) are projected to reinforce regional expansion and service levels. On the energy side the Company has increased reliance on renewable sources through long-term open access agreements aggregating to 12,375 KW along with solar energy sourcing through various modes of 16,167 kWp, with solar now more than 55% of total electricity consumption. Management frames the outlook as a transition from consolidation to "calibrated growth and strategic expansion", with ongoing brownfield FIBC capacity expansion as the primary growth driver and geographic expansion beyond Europe into North America, South America and Japan.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Management states the FIBC industry outlook is expected to remain positive, driven by growth in global trade, industrial packaging demand, supply chain diversification, and preference for sustainable bulk packaging solutions.
- Demand across key end-user industries is described as remaining structurally positive, particularly in regulated and compliance-driven markets, even while global macroeconomic conditions and geopolitical developments continue to create uncertainties.
- Customers are increasingly prioritizing traceability, regulatory compliance, customization and sustainable solutions over commoditized volumes, reinforcing the importance of engineering excellence, operational agility and pricing discipline — the areas where the Company says it differentiates.
- A structural shift is under way in the method of FIBC sales, which are moving from B2B to B2C on a gradual basis.
- The ongoing capacity expansion in the FIBC segment is expected to support volume growth and enhance operating efficiencies, and the proposed FIBC capacity expansion is expected to further improve the product mix.
- FY 2025-26 performance drivers cited by management were improved realizations, operating leverage and a higher contribution from premium products; the Company reports focus on value-added products and customer retention yielded stable volume but higher sales realizations.
- Export focus, supported by deeper customer engagement and improved market access, is expected to provide stability and growth opportunities.
- Evolving tariff structures and geopolitical developments may continue to influence sourcing strategies across international markets; despite the onset of US tariffs the share of the USA in the Company's FIBC exports dropped only marginally and was more than offset by increased penetration in the EU and steps taken in other geographies.
- India continues to strengthen its position as the leading global supplier of FIBCs, accounting in 2025 for nearly 78.2% of FIBC imports in the United States, 50.0% in Canada and 66.4% in the European Union, while China's share in global FIBC exports continued to decline on changing trade dynamics and tariffs and Vietnam and Bangladesh increased their presence particularly in North America.
- Global international trade in FIBCs during 2025 is estimated at over US$ 1.75 billion, 65% of which is accounted for by imports within the USA, Canada and the EU countries.
- Global plastic packaging market growth is driven by heightened regulatory scrutiny, rising convenience food consumption, cost-competitive advantages over alternative substrates and an accelerating shift toward sustainability; drivers listed are growing demand from pharma, food and personal care, advances in processing technology and packaging materials, and growth of consumer electronics and appliances, with restraints of stringent environmental regulations and volatile raw material prices and opportunities in sustainable/recyclable materials and circular economy initiatives.
- Indian plastic packaging regulation is tightening, but management states Kanpur Plastipack's export production remains outside the ambit of these regulatory conditions.
- Certifications (food-grade, SEDEX, Kosher, Halal, BRCGS A+, HACCP) and traceability/compliance frameworks are described as increasingly essential for servicing global and consumer-facing customers and as strengthening presence in value-added, premium and regulated segments.
- Entry into technical textiles via the non-woven project is framed as a conscious diversification into B2C-linked opportunities such as automotive interiors, lifestyle products, filter fabrics and geo textiles, marking a gradual shift from purely industrial applications.
- The DOPW activity of IOCL witnessed a strong recovery, responding positively to new Company initiatives and to the new DOP warehouse opened at Bareily in the previous year.
- Export mix by geography during the year: Europe accounted for 56.5% of exports, followed by South America at 21.8% and North America at 16.9%, with continued strong presence in EU countries, USA and Brazil.
- FIBC is stated to account for approximately 53% of total manufacturing revenues, and international demand, increased operational efficiencies across manufacturing units and expansion into new markets shaped segment performance.
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Kanpur Plastipack navigated FY26 raw material volatility (PP prices up 65%) via disciplined pricing and a strategic pivot toward higher-margin non-woven technical textiles, delivering 68% PAT growth despite a one-off DFIA reversal. The imminent commissioning of non-woven capacity (Sep '26) and FIBC expansion (Unit 3) sets the stage for a structural re-rating from a pure-play FIBC exporter to a diversified technical textile solutions provider.

open.item: H1 FY26 margins (Q2 EBITDA margin 9.8%) expected to remain sustainable and possibly move up, driven by volumes and diversification.
H2 FY26 revenue and margins expected to remain similar to H1 (H1 EBITDA ~INR32cr).
FIBC capacity 18,000 tons with utilisation currently 82% (14,500 tons), expected to reach 85-86% by H2 exit.
Company plans to cut total outstanding debt from INR190 crore to about INR125 crore by end of FY26 (term loan INR80cr->INR15cr, WC INR120cr->INR110cr).
EBITDA percentages are expected to remain broadly the same over the next three quarters, with demand and order book supportive.
Valex Ventures to add a net INR4-5 crore to consolidated top line, with contributions starting from the next quarter.
Valex Ventures revenue (GBP 1.1m FY25) expected at GBP 1.2-1.3m this year and to grow 5-10% every year thereafter.
Management guided that the sustainable EBITDA margin will remain between 9% and 10% going forward.
50-50 Essegomma JV (Taslan high-performance yarn) to reach commercial production by Q1 next FY, generating ~INR25 crore annual revenue in first couple of years.
Grant Thornton engaged on risk/advisory to streamline processes and drive productivity; reports expected over next 6-12 months as an ongoing exercise.
The Company proposes to add capacity in its weaving section and Multi Filament Yarn (MFY) division to cater to future requirements of these segments.

Total expenditure on the technical-textiles diversification and capacity-expansion projects will amount to Rs 107 Cr and is expected to be completed by September 2026, part-funded by a Rs 40 Cr term loan taken from Yes Bank.

Establish a greenfield non-woven fabrics manufacturing facility based on needle-punching technology in the existing building from the erstwhile CPP division, with plant and equipment arriving from June 2026 and commercial production starting by September 2026.
Total expenditure on the non-woven project plus the capacity-expansion and infrastructure projects will amount to Rs 107 Cr and is expected to be completed by September 2026.

Greenfield non-woven fabrics facility (needle-punching technology, re-using the erstwhile CPP division building) — plant and equipment to start arriving from June 2026 with commercial production to start by September 2026.

Total expenditure on the non-woven diversification project plus the FIBC/weaving/MFY capacity expansion and infrastructure programme will amount to Rs. 107 Cr and is expected to be completed by September 2026.

Greenfield non-woven fabrics facility based on needle-punching technology: plant and equipment is expected to start arriving from June 2026 onwards with commercial production to start by September 2026 (the MD's message states commercial production targeted to commence from FY 2026-27).

The Board has re-appointed Shri Manoj Agarwal as Chairman cum Managing Director for a further period of three years with effect from 01 September 2026 on fresh terms, subject to shareholder approval at the ensuing Annual General Meeting.
Warehouse expansion and automation initiatives underway, expected to be completed by September (FY27).
Non-woven technical textile commercial production to commence by September FY27 (first machine Sept, second machine December).

wtt.summary: Building track record — 3Q logged, no reconciled verdicts yet.
wtt.tone_latest: Measured and disciplined, framing FY26 as a year of transition and consolidation; management openly flagged the DFIA reversal (INR3.65cr), raw-material spike and softer order book while reaffirming margin resilience.
